en: Dīgha Nikāya 13:
The Discourse on the Threefold Knowledge (Tevijjasutta) Thus have I heard—

On one occasion, while the Blessed One was wandering on tour among the Kosalans with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus, numbering about five hundred bhikkhus, he arrived at a brahmin village of the Kosalans named Manasākaṭa.
There the Blessed One stayed at Manasākaṭa, to the north of Manasākaṭa, in a mango grove on the bank of the river Aciravatī.
Now at that time, many well-known and distinguished wealthy brahmins were residing at Manasākaṭa, such as: [The names of the brahmins follow.]
The brahmin Caṅki, the brahmin Tārukkha, the brahmin Pokkharasāti, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi, the brahmin Todeyya, and other well-known and renowned wealthy brahmins.
Then, as the young brahmins Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja were walking and wandering along for exercise, a discussion arose between them concerning what is the path and what is not the path.
Then the young brahmin Vāseṭṭha spoke thus:
“This indeed is the straight path, this is the direct way that leads out, leading the one who practices it to companionship with Brahmā—this which was proclaimed by the brahmin Pokkharasāti.
The young Brahmin Bhāradvāja also spoke thus:
“This indeed is the straight path, this is the direct way that leads out, leading the one who practices it to companionship with Brahmā—this which was proclaimed by the brahmin Tārukkha.”
Vāseṭṭha the young brahmin was unable to convince Bhāradvāja the young brahmin, nor was Bhāradvāja the young brahmin able to convince Vāseṭṭha the young brahmin.
Then Vāseṭṭha the young brahmin addressed Bhāradvāja the young brahmin:

"Bhāradvāja, this ascetic Gotama, a son of the Sakyans who went forth from the Sakyan clan, is staying at Manasākaṭa, to the north of Manasākaṭa, on the bank of the river Aciravatī in the Mango Grove."
Furthermore, this excellent report concerning the venerable Gotama has spread abroad:

"Indeed, that Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Come, Master Bhāradvāja, let us approach the ascetic Gotama; having approached him, we shall ask the ascetic Gotama about this matter.
“Whatever the ascetic Gotama explains to us, we shall hold it in that way.
“So be it, sir,” the young Brahmin Bhāradvāja replied to the young Brahmin Vāseṭṭha.
1. The Discourse on the Path and the Non-Path.
Then the young brahmins Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
When they had concluded their courteous and memorable conversation, they sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the young brahmin Vāseṭṭha said this to the Blessed One:
"Here, Master Gotama, while we were walking and wandering for exercise along a path, a discussion arose among us concerning what is the right path and what is not."
"I myself say this:
'This alone is the straight path, this is the direct way that leads out, leading the one who practices it to companionship with Brahmā—this which was proclaimed by the brahmin Pokkharasāti.
The young Brahmin Bhāradvāja spoke thus."
“This alone is the straight path, this is the direct way that leads out, leading the one who practices it to companionship with Brahmā—this which has been proclaimed by the brahmin Tārukkha.
“In this matter, Master Gotama, there is indeed dispute, there is contention, there is disagreement.
“So you say, Vāseṭṭha?”
“This alone is the straight path, this is the direct way that leads out, leading the practitioner to companionship with Brahmā—this is what was proclaimed by the brahmin Pokkharasāti.
Thus spoke the young Brahmin Bhāradvāja:
“This alone is the straight path, this is the direct way that leads out, leading the practitioner to companionship with Brahmā—this is what was proclaimed by the brahmin Tārukkha.”
“But in what, Vāseṭṭha, is there dispute for you, in what is there contention, in what is there disagreement?
“In the path and the non-path, Master Gotama.
For although, Master Gotama, the brahmins prescribe various paths—the Addhariya brahmins, the Tittiriya...”
"Brāhmaṇas who are Vedic chanters, brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas, and brāhmaṇas who are learned in the scriptures—all of these lead to liberation;
they lead the practitioner to companionship with Brahmā.
Just as, Master Gotama, if there are many different roads not far from a village or a town, they all nevertheless converge upon that village."
"In the same way, Master Gotama, although the brahmins prescribe various paths— the Addhariya brahmins,
the Tittiriya brahmins, the Chandoka brahmins, and the Bavhārija brahmins— nevertheless,
they are all leading outwards; they lead the one who practices them to companionship with Brahmā."
2. The Discourse on the Young Brahmin Vāseṭṭha:
“Vāseṭṭha, do you say they lead out?
“I say they lead out, Master Gotama.”
“Do you say, Vāseṭṭha, ‘they lead out’?
“I say, Master Gotama, ‘they lead out.
“Do you say, Vāseṭṭha, ‘they lead out’?”
“They lead out, Master Gotama, so I say.
“But, Vāseṭṭha, is there even a single one among the Brahmins learned in the Three Vedas who has seen Brahmā face to face?
“Certainly not, Master Gotama.”
“But then, Vāseṭṭha, is there even a single teacher among the Brahmins learned in the three Vedas who has seen Brahmā face to face?
“No indeed, Master Gotama.
“But then, Vāseṭṭha, is there even a single teacher of a teacher among the Brahmins learned in the three Vedas who has seen Brahmā face to face?”
“No, Master Gotama.

“But what do you think, Vāseṭṭha? Is there any among the Brahmins learned in the three Vedas who, reaching back through seven generations of teachers and their pupils, has ever seen Brahmā face to face?
“No, Master Gotama.”
“But what do you think, Vāseṭṭha? As for those ancient seers of the brahmins learned in the three Vedas— the makers of the mantras, the proclaimers of the mantras,
whose ancient mantra-words are now chanted, proclaimed, and compiled by the brahmins learned in the three Vedas today,
whom they chant along with, repeat after, recite as spoken, and teach as taught— namely, Aṭṭhaka...”
“Vāmaka, Vāmadeva, Vessāmitta, Yamataggi, Aṅgīrasa, Bhāradvāja, Vāseṭṭha, Kassapa, and Bhagu—they too said this:
‘We know this, we see this: where Brahmā is, by what means Brahmā is reached, and in what state Brahmā dwells.’”
“No, Master Gotama.
“Thus it seems, Vāseṭṭha, that among these Brahmins learned in the three Vedas, there is not even a single Brahmin who has seen Brahmā face to face.
Nor is there even a single teacher among these Brahmins learned in the three Vedas who has seen Brahmā face to face.”
Among those Brahmins learned in the three Vedas, there is not even a single teacher of teachers who has seen Brahmā face-to-face.
Among those Brahmins learned in the three Vedas, there is no one—even reaching back through seven generations of teachers and their predecessors—who has seen Brahmā face-to-face.
Even as for those ancient seers of the Brahmins learned in the three Vedas, the authors of the mantras and the transmitters of the mantras—
Those ancient Vedic verses that have been chanted, uttered, and compiled— which the Brahmins learned in the three Vedas today sing along with,
repeat after, recite as they were spoken, and teach as they were taught, namely those of Aṭṭhaka, Vāmaka, Vāmadeva, Vessāmitta,
Yamataggi, Aṅgīrasa, Bhāradvāja, Vāseṭṭha, Kassapa, and Bhagu— even they did not say this:
‘We know this, we see this: where Brahmā is, by what means Brahmā is reached, and in whatever state Brahmā exists.
Yet those brahmins possessing the threefold knowledge speak thus:
‘We teach the path to companionship with that which we do not know and do not see.’
“This alone is the straight path, this is the direct way that leads out, leading the one who practices it to companionship with Brahmā.
What do you think, Vāseṭṭha,
is it not the case that, this being so, the speech of the Brahmins learned in the three Vedas turns out to be without foundation?”
“Certainly, Master Gotama, that being so, the speech of the Brahmins learned in the three Vedas turns out to be without foundation.
“Good, Vāseṭṭha! Indeed, Vāseṭṭha, those Brahmins learned in the three Vedas would teach the path for companionship with that which they do not know and do not see, saying:
‘This alone is the straight path, this is the direct way that leads out.’”
‘...it leads the practitioner to companionship with Brahmā’—this is impossible.

Just as, Vāseṭṭha, a file of blind men clinging together—neither the first, nor the middle one, nor the last one sees—so too, Vāseṭṭha, I consider the speech of the Brahmins learned in the Three Vedas to be like a file of blind men: neither the first, nor the middle one, nor the last one sees.
“The speech of these brahmins who claim to possess the threefold knowledge turns out to be merely laughable, merely nominal, empty, and hollow.
What do you think, Vāseṭṭha?

Do these brahmins who claim to possess the threefold knowledge see the sun and moon—where the sun and moon rise from and where they set—and do they invoke them, praise them, and circumambulate them with joined palms in worship?”
“Indeed, Master Gotama, the brahmins learned in the three Vedas, as well as many other people, see the moon and the sun;
and from where the moon and the sun rise, and where they set, they pray, praise,
and circumambulate them with hands joined in reverence.”
“What do you think, Vāseṭṭha?
When the brahmins learned in the three Vedas, as well as many other people, see the sun and moon— where the sun and moon rise and where they set—
and when they invoke them, praise them, and circumambulate them with joined palms in worship;”
“Are the brahmins learned in the three Vedas able to point out the path to companionship with the moon and sun, saying:
‘This alone is the straight path, this is the direct way that leads out; it leads the one who practices it to companionship with the moon and sun’?
“Certainly not, Master Gotama.”
“Thus, Vāseṭṭha, it seems that even those brahmins learned in the three Vedas— who see the sun and moon, and who,
from where the sun and moon rise to where they set, invoke them, praise them, and circumambulate them with palms joined in reverence—
even for them it is not possible to show the path to companionship with the sun and moon.”
"This alone is the straight path, this is the direct way that leads out, leading the one who practices it to companionship with the moon and sun.
Yet, it is said that Brahmā has not been seen face-to-face by the Brahmins learned in the Three Vedas,
nor has Brahmā been seen face-to-face by the teachers of those Brahmins learned in the Three Vedas.
It seems that Brahmā has not been seen by personal witness even by the teachers and sub-teachers of the Brahmins learned in the three Vedas.
It seems that Brahmā has not been seen by personal witness even by the Brahmins learned in the three Vedas as far back as the seventh generation of teachers.
And it seems that even those ancient seers of the Brahmins learned in the three Vedas, the makers of the mantras and the transmitters of the mantras—
Those ancient brahmins of the threefold knowledge for whom these verses of the mantras were sung, uttered, and compiled, which they now sing along with,
recite along with, repeat what was spoken, and teach what was taught— namely, Aṭṭhaka,
Vāmaka, Vāmadeva, Vessāmitta, Yamataggi, Aṅgīrasa, Bhāradvāja, Vāseṭṭha, Kassapa, and Bhagu— even they did not say this:
‘We know this, we see this: where Brahmā is, by what means Brahmā is reached, and in what state Brahmā dwells.
Yet those Brahmins learned in the three Vedas say this:

‘Regarding that which we do not know and that which we do not see, we teach the path to its companionship—this very straight path, this direct way, is leading, it leads the practitioner to companionship with Brahmā.’”
“What do you think, Vāseṭṭha,
does it not follow, this being so, that the speech of the Brahmins learned in the three Vedas turns out to be without foundation?
“Certainly, Master Gotama, this being so, the speech of the Brahmins learned in the three Vedas turns out to be without foundation.”
“Excellent, Vāseṭṭha! It is indeed impossible, Vāseṭṭha, that those Brahmins learned in the three Vedas would teach the path to the companionship of that which they neither know nor see, saying:
‘This alone is the straight path, this is the direct way leading out;
it leads the one who practices it to the companionship of Brahmā. Such a thing cannot be.”
2.1. The Simile of the Most Beautiful Woman in the Land.
“Vāseṭṭha, suppose a man were to say:
‘I desire her, I long for her—she who is the most beautiful woman in this land.’”
They would say to him:
"O man, regarding that woman who is the most beautiful in the land whom you desire and love,
do you know whether that woman who is the most beautiful in the land is a kṣatriya, a brahmin, a vaiśya, or a śūdrā?"
Being asked thus, he would say, ‘No.
Then they would say to him:
‘Good man, do you know that beautiful woman of the land whom you desire and lust after—her name being such-and-such?’
‘Is his clan such-and-such? or ‘Is he tall, or short, or of medium height? or ‘Is he dark, or fair, or of golden skin?
or ‘Does he live in such-and-such a village, town, or city?
Being asked thus, he would say, ‘No.’”
They would say to him:
"O man, do you desire and long for that which you neither know nor see?
Being thus questioned, he would answer: "Yes."
“What do you think, Vāseṭṭha, when this is so,
does that man’s speech not turn out to be unconvincing?
“Certainly, Master Gotama, when this is so, that man’s speech turns out to be unconvincing.”
“In the same way, Vāseṭṭha, it seems that Brahmā has not been seen by the Brahmins learned in the three Vedas,
nor has Brahmā been seen by the teachers of the Brahmins learned in the three Vedas, nor has Brahmā been seen by the teachers of the teachers of the Brahmins learned in the three Vedas.”
It seems that even among the Brahmins learned in the three Vedas, Brahmā has not been seen face-to-face by anyone within seven generations of teachers and grand-teachers.
Furthermore, it seems that even those ancient seers of the Brahmins learned in the three Vedas— who were the authors of the mantras and the propagators of the mantras,
whose ancient mantra-words the Brahmins learned in the three Vedas now sing, recite, and rehearse— [have not seen him].

They repeat what he has said, they repeat what was spoken, they recite what was recited—namely, Aṭṭhaka, Vāmaka, Vāmadeva, Vessāmitta, Yamataggi, Aṅgīrasa, Bhāradvāja, Vāseṭṭha, Kassapa, and Bhagu. Yet even they did not say:
"We know this, we see this—where Brahmā is, by whom Brahmā is, or in what way Brahmā exists."
Those very same Brahmins learned in the three Vedas say this:

“We teach the path to the companionship of that which we do not know and have not seen—‘This alone is the straight path, this is the direct way, leading out; it leads the one who practices it to the companionship of Brahmā.
What do you think, Vāseṭṭha, does this not result in the speech of the Brahmins learned in the three Vedas being without foundation?”
“Certainly, Master Gotama, that being so, the speech of the brahmins who claim to possess the threefold knowledge turns out to be without foundation.

“Excellent, Vāseṭṭha! It would indeed be excellent, Vāseṭṭha, if those brahmins who claim to possess the threefold knowledge were to teach the path for the sake of companionship with that which they do not know and do not see—saying:
‘This alone is the straight path, this is the direct way; it leads out, it leads to liberation.’”
"For one who acts thus, companionship with Brahmā—this is impossible.
2.2. The Simile of the Ladder:
"Vāseṭṭha, it is just as if a man were to construct a ladder at a crossroads for the purpose of ascending to a palace."
They would say to him: "O man, do you know that palace for which you are making a ladder to ascend it—
whether it is high, low, or middling in height, and whether it stands in the eastern direction, the southern direction, the western direction, or the northern direction?"
Being asked thus, he would say, "No. Then they would say to him:
"O man, you are building a ladder for the ascent of that palace which you neither know nor see!"
Being asked thus, he would say, “Yes.
What do you think, Vāseṭṭha,
in that case, would the speech of that man not turn out to be unconvincing?”
“Certainly, Master Gotama, that being the case, the speech of that man turns out to be unconvincing.
“In the same way, Vāseṭṭha, it seems that Brahmā has not been seen by the Brahmins learned in the Three Vedas,
nor has Brahmā been seen by the teachers of the Brahmins learned in the Three Vedas, nor indeed by the Brahmins learned in the Three Vedas themselves.”

Brahmā has been seen face-to-face by teachers of teachers; it is said that Brahmā has not been seen face-to-face even by the Brahmins learned in the three Vedas, reaching back through seven generations of their teachers and great-uncles.
Even those ancient seers of the Brahmins learned in the three Vedas, the authors of the mantras and the transmitters of the mantras—

Those brahmins of the threefold knowledge who nowadays chant, recite, repeat what has been spoken, and teach what has been taught— the ancient verses of the mantras that were sung, uttered, and compiled, namely those of Aṭṭhaka,
Vāmaka, Vāmadeva, Vessāmitta, Yamataggi, Aṅgīrasa, Bhāradvāja, Vāseṭṭha, Kassapa, and Bhagu— even they did not say this:
"We know this, we see this: where Brahmā is, by what means Brahmā is reached, and in what state Brahmā exists.
Yet those Brahmins possessing the threefold knowledge say this:

"We shall teach the path to the companionship of that which we do not know and do not see; this alone is the straight path, this is the direct way, leading out, leading the practitioner to the companionship of Brahmā."
"What do you think, Vāseṭṭha? Is it not the case that, this being so, the speech of the Brahmins learned in the three Vedas turns out to be without foundation?
"Certainly, Master Gotama, this being so, the speech of the Brahmins learned in the three Vedas turns out to be without foundation.
"Good, Vāseṭṭha! Indeed, Vāseṭṭha, those Brahmins learned in the three Vedas [speak] of what they do not know and what they do not see."
They will teach the path to his companionship, saying: "This is the straight path, this is the direct way that leads out;
it leads the one who practices it to companionship with Brahmā. This is impossible.
2.3. The Simile of the River Aciravatī.
"Just as, Vāseṭṭha, this river Aciravatī is full of water, brimming to the top so that a crow could drink from it;
then a man might come along, desiring the further shore, seeking the further shore, going toward the further shore, wishing to cross over to the further shore.
Standing on this bank, he would call out to the further bank:"
“Come from the far shore to this shore!

Come from this shore to the far shore! What do you think, Vāseṭṭha, would that person’s far shore of the Aciravatī River come to this shore on account of his calling, or his praying, or his aspiring, or his longing?”
“Certainly not, Master Gotama.

“In the very same way, Vāseṭṭha, those Brahmins learned in the three Vedas, while abandoning those qualities that make one a Brahmin and adopting those qualities that do not make one a Brahmin, say this:
‘We invoke Indra! We invoke Soma! We invoke Varuṇa! We invoke Īśāna! We invoke Pajāpati! We invoke Brahmā! We invoke Mahiddhi! We invoke Yama!’”
Indeed, Vāseṭṭha, those Brahmins learned in the three Vedas— who, while practicing by abandoning those qualities that make one a Brahmin,
yet adopting and practicing those qualities that do not make one a Brahmin— might, for the sake of an invitation, for the sake of a request, for the sake of a wish,
or for the sake of approval, upon the breakup of the body after death, go to the company of Brahmā.
that they will come into being—this is impossible.
Vāseṭṭha, it is just as if this river Aciravatī were full of water, brimming to the top so that a crow could drink from it.
Then a man might come along, seeking the far shore, searching for the far shore, going toward the far shore, desiring to cross over to the far shore.
"Suppose, Vāseṭṭha, that man were tied with a strong rope behind his back on this bank of the river, with his arms held tightly fast.
What do you think, Vāseṭṭha,
would that man be able to go from the near bank of the river Aciravatī to the far bank?"
“No, Master Gotama.

“In the same way, Vāseṭṭha, these five cords of sensual pleasure are called ‘fetters’ and ‘bonds’ in the discipline of the Noble One. Which five? [The passage continues with the description of the five cords of sensual pleasure.]”
Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.
Sounds cognizable by the ear … smells cognizable by the nose … [and so on] … [as above].
Tastes cognizable by the tongue...
tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, and provocative of lust.
These, Vāseṭṭha, are the five cords of sensual pleasure which, in the discipline of the Noble One, are called "fetters" and are also called "bonds."
"Vāseṭṭha, these brahmins learned in the three Vedas, being infatuated with, obsessed by, and deeply attached to these five strands of sensual pleasure—
failing to see their danger and lacking wisdom regarding the escape from them— make use of them. Indeed, Vāseṭṭha, those brahmins learned in the three Vedas,

while abandoning those qualities that make one a brahmin and adopting and practicing those qualities that do not make one a brahmin, remain infatuated with and obsessed by the five strands of sensual pleasure."
"Vāseṭṭha, it is impossible that those who enjoy [sensual pleasures] while being obsessed by them, failing to see the danger and lacking the wisdom for escape,
yet bound by the fetter of craving, should— upon the breakup of the body, after death— attain companionship with the Brahmās. It is just as if, Vāseṭṭha,
this river Aciravatī were full of water, brimming to the brim so that a crow could drink from it."
Then, suppose a man were to come along seeking the further shore, searching for the further shore, going toward the further shore, desiring to cross over to the further shore.
He would lie down on this near shore with his head covered.
What do you think, Vāseṭṭha?
“Would that man, Vāseṭṭha, go from the near bank of the river Aciravatī to the far bank?
“No indeed, Master Gotama.
“In the same way, Vāseṭṭha, these five hindrances are in the discipline of the Noble One called obstructions, they are called hindrances, they are called coverings, and they are called envelopments.”
Which five?
The hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt.
These, Vāseṭṭha, in the discipline of the Noble One, are called hindrances, they are called obstructions, they are called coverings, and they are called envelopments.
"Vāseṭṭha, by these five hindrances the brahmins who are masters of the three Vedas are obstructed, shut in, enveloped, and hemmed in. Indeed, Vāseṭṭha,
while those brahmins who are masters of the three Vedas are living having abandoned those qualities that make one a brahmin and having adopted those qualities that do not make one a brahmin,
they remain obstructed, shut in, enveloped, and hemmed in by the five hindrances."
"Clad and covered [in finery], with the breakup of the body, after death, they will go to the company of the Brahmās"—this is impossible.
3. Discourse on Corroboration.
“What do you think, Vāseṭṭha, what have you heard from the aged and elderly brahmins, the teachers of teachers, as they were speaking: is Brahmā possessed of a wife, or is he without a wife?
“He is without a wife, Master Gotama.”
“Is his mind free from enmity or possessed of enmity?
“His mind is free from enmity, Master Gotama.
“Is his mind free from ill will or possessed of ill will?”
“His mind is free from ill will, Master Gotama.
“Is his mind defiled or undefiled?
“It is undefiled, Master Gotama.”
“Is he one who has mastery or one who lacks mastery?
“He has mastery, Master Gotama.
“What do you think, Vāseṭṭha?”
“Are the brahmins who possess the threefold knowledge possessed of attachments, or are they without attachments?
“They are possessed of attachments, Master Gotama.
“Do they have minds full of enmity, or are their minds free from enmity?”
“With a mind full of malice, Master Gotama.
“Is their mind full of ill will or free from ill will?
“It is full of ill will, Master Gotama.”
“Is their mind defiled or undefiled?
“Defiled, Master Gotama.
“Do they have mastery over it or do they lack mastery?”
“Not under his control, Master Gotama.
“In that case, Vāseṭṭha, the threefold-knowledge brahmins possess possessions, whereas Brahmā is without possessions.
Would it not be the case that those threefold-knowledge brahmins who possess possessions do not harmonize or coincide with Brahmā, who is without possessions?”
“No, Master Gotama. “Good, Vāseṭṭha.

Indeed, Vāseṭṭha, it is impossible that those brahmins learned in the three Vedas, who possess property, should, with the breakup of the body, after death, go to the company of Brahmā, who is without property.
Thus, Vāseṭṭha, it seems that the brahmins learned in the three Vedas have minds full of enmity, whereas Brahmā has a mind free from enmity…” [and so on].

“Brahmā has a mind free from ill will, whereas the Brahmins learned in the three Vedas have minds with ill will… Brahmā has a mind that is undefiled, whereas the Brahmins learned in the three Vedas have defiled minds… Brahmā exercises mastery,

whereas the Brahmins learned in the three Vedas do not exercise mastery. Now, would those Brahmins learned in the three Vedas, who do not exercise mastery, meet and coincide with Brahmā, who exercises mastery?”
“No, Master Gotama. “Good, Vāseṭṭha.

Indeed, Vāseṭṭha, it is impossible that those Brahmins learned in the three Vedas, being powerless over themselves, should, with the breakup of the body, after death, attain companionship with Brahmā, who is powerful.

On the contrary, Vāseṭṭha, having sat down here, those Brahmins learned in the three Vedas sink; having sunk, they reach a state of drifting, as if they were trying to cross a place that is even drier.”

“Therefore, this [failure] of the Brahmins who possess the threefold knowledge is called a desert for the threefold knowledge, a wilderness for the threefold knowledge, and a calamity for the threefold knowledge.
When this was said, the young Brahmin Vāseṭṭha said to the Blessed One:
“I have heard this, Master Gotama: ‘The ascetic Gotama knows the path to the company of Brahmā.’”
“What do you think, Vāseṭṭha?
Is Manasākaṭa near here, or is Manasākaṭa far from here?
“Yes, Master Gotama, Manasākaṭa is near here; Manasākaṭa is not far from here.”
“What do you think, Vāseṭṭha?
Suppose there were a man born and raised in Manasākaṭa,
and immediately after leaving Manasākaṭa, they were to ask him the way to Manasākaṭa.”
“Vāseṭṭha, would there be any hesitation or delay for that man, born and raised in Manasākaṭa, when asked about the road to Manasākaṭa?
“No indeed, Master Gotama. “And why is that?”
“Indeed, Master Gotama, that man was born and raised in Manasākaṭa; therefore, all the roads to Manasākaṭa are well known to him.

“It may be, Vāseṭṭha, that for that man born and raised in Manasākaṭa there might be some hesitation or delay when asked about the road to Manasākaṭa, but it could never be so for the Tathāgata regarding the Brahmā-world.”
“Or, Vāseṭṭha, when asked about the practice leading to the world of Brahmā, there would be either hesitation or prolixity.

But I, Vāseṭṭha, understand the Brahmās, the world of Brahmā, and the practice leading to the world of Brahmā; and I understand how one who has practiced accordingly has been reborn in the world of Brahmā.
When this was said, the young Brahmin Vāseṭṭha addressed the Blessed One as follows:
“I have heard this, Master Gotama: ‘The ascetic Gotama teaches the path to companionship with Brahmā.
It would be well if Master Gotama would teach us the path to companionship with Brahmā; may Master Gotama uplift this generation of brahmins.
“In that case, Vāseṭṭha, listen and pay close attention; I shall speak.”
“Yes, sir,” the young brahmin Vāseṭṭha replied to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One spoke as follows: 4. The Teaching on the Path to the Brahma World The Blessed One said this: [text continues]
“Here, Vāseṭṭha, a Tathāgata arises in the world, an arahant, perfectly enlightened...
Thus, Vāseṭṭha, a bhikkhu is accomplished in virtue...

When he perceives within himself that these five hindrances have been abandoned, gladness is born; in one who is glad, rapture is born; for one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; with a tranquil body, one experiences happiness; and for one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated.
Thus, with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, he dwells pervading one quarter; likewise the second, likewise the third, and likewise the fourth.

Thus above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—vast, exalted, measureless, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
"Just as, Vāseṭṭha, a powerful conch-blower might easily make himself heard in all four directions,
even so, Vāseṭṭha, when the liberation of mind through loving-kindness has been developed in this way, whatever limited kamma there may be does not remain there,
nor does it persist there. This, Vāseṭṭha, is the path to the company of Brahmās."
Furthermore, Vāseṭṭha, a bhikkhu dwells pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with compassion...
with a mind imbued with sympathetic joy...
with a mind imbued with equanimity; likewise the second quarter, likewise the third.

In the same way, the fourth [jhāna]. Thus, above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwells having pervaded the entire world with a mind accompanied by equanimity—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
Just as, Vāseṭṭha, a powerful conch-blower might easily make himself heard in the four quarters;
In the same way, Vāseṭṭha, when the liberation of mind through equanimity has been thus developed, whatever limited karma there may be does not remain there, nor does it persist there.
This, Vāseṭṭha, is the path to the company of the Brahmās.
What do you think, Vāseṭṭha?
“Does a bhikkhu who dwells in such a way possess attachments or not?”—
“He is without attachments, Master Gotama.”—
“Does he have a mind full of enmity or a mind free from enmity?”— [“He has a mind free from enmity, Master Gotama.”]
“He is without ill will, Master Gotama.
“Is his mind full of malice or free from malice?
“His mind is free from malice, Master Gotama.”
“Is his mind defiled or undefiled?
“It is undefiled, Master Gotama.
“Does he have mastery over it or does he not have mastery over it?”
“Powerful, Master Gotama.
“In that case, Vāseṭṭha, since the bhikkhu is without possessions and Brahmā is without possessions,
does the bhikkhu without possessions come together with and meet the Brahmā without possessions?”
“Yes, Master Gotama.

“Excellent, Vāseṭṭha! Indeed, Vāseṭṭha, it is possible that a bhikkhu who is without acquisitions, with the breakup of the body, after death, will reappear in the company of Brahmā, who is without acquisitions.
Thus, Vāseṭṭha, it seems that a bhikkhu whose mind is free from enmity [will reappear in the company of] Brahmā, whose mind is free from enmity... [and so on].
“A bhikkhu with a mind free from ill will, a Brahmā with a mind free from ill will… a bhikkhu with an undefiled mind,

a Brahmā with an undefiled mind… a bhikkhu who wields mastery, a Brahmā who wields mastery— would it not be the case that the bhikkhu who wields mastery meets and coincides with the Brahmā who wields mastery?”
“Yes, Master Gotama.
“Excellent, Vāseṭṭha! Indeed, Vāseṭṭha, it is possible that a bhikkhu who wields power, with the breakup of the body, after death, will reappear in the company of the Brahmā Vasavattī.
When this was said, the young brahmins Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja said this to the Blessed One:
“Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama!

Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms; [so it has been done by Master Gotama].”
"In this very way, the Dhamma has been proclaimed by Master Gotama in many ways.
We go for refuge to Master Gotama, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May Master Gotama accept us as lay followers who have gone for refuge from this day forth as long as life shall last."
The *Tevijja-sutta* is finished; it is the thirteenth.
The *Sīlakkhandha-vagga* is finished.
Here is its summary verse (*uddāna*):
Brahmā, Sāmaññaphala, Ambaṭṭha, Soṇadaṇḍa,
Kūṭadanta, Mahāli, Jāliya, Sīha,
Poṭṭhapāda, Subha, and Kevaṭṭa.
The thirteen *Lohiccavijjā* [discourses].
The text of the Sīlakkhandha-vagga is concluded.
